epics.title: Harness Training Loop
epics.description:
The pivot: the harness is the target, the app is the fixture. The subject of improvement is no longer hive-health — it is the harness and the scaffolding around a small model, with the app demoted to a fixture that produces signal. A second throwaway project is created with the same requirements as hive-health, and a small model driven by a lightweight harness is told to build that app from the behaviour manifest alone. It cannot see the original source. Every failure it hits is a signal, and what gets rewritten in response is the harness, the prompts, the standing rules and the skills — never the model's output.

The captured manifest is still the oracle, unchanged. What changed is what it grades: not whether a refactor preserved behaviour but whether a rebuild satisfies the spec. The throwaway target means behaviour preservation is irrelevant and conformance takes its place, which is a larger and less gameable signal than a duplication count.

The problem it targets: AI-generated code is locally sufficient and globally incoherent. A feature works, but viewed against the rest of the app it duplicates logic that already existed, ignores a shared helper and rewrites it single-purpose, and wastes resources nothing was watching. The loop's job is the step back nobody takes — reduce total code, consolidate duplicates, reuse what exists, and leave behaviour untouched.

The deliverable is the harness. A harness good enough to hand a weak model is what gets kept. The fine-tune is deferred indefinitely and is better suited to the work setting, with more developers on it, than to this workstation. Nothing in the design depends on it happening.
epics.requirements:
The two loops fight each other, so they are phased strictly. Harness hardening is a tool call that errors, a tool that is missing, a schema the model cannot satisfy — unambiguous, mechanical and immediately valuable, where a large model reads the failure and rewrites the adapter with no training involved. Scaffolding hardening is where the harness works and the model still makes mistakes — wrong tool for the job, skipped a skill it should have read, wrong output shape — and a large model rewrites prompts, standing rules or skills. Fine-tuning is rejection-sampling fine-tuning, a real technique rather than a fantasy: run many attempts, keep the ones that pass the oracle, train on those. The trap is that it is in direct tension with the first loop, because every harness fix makes the small model succeed for reasons that are not in the model, so a trace collected while the harness is still being repaired teaches the model nothing it can carry. So: harden the harness and the scaffolding first with no training, then freeze both, and only then collect traces — because from that point a success is attributable to the model and a failure is the model's own.

Isolation rather than cleverness prevents reward hacking: the builder runs in a container whose filesystem holds the empty project directory and the behaviour manifest and nothing else — no hive-health checkout, no git remote, no network path to the original — and the oracle runs outside that container. Nothing needs to be hidden by prompt instruction, because nothing is reachable.

Nothing that measures is writable by the model. Every metric is gameable precisely when the model can edit the thing doing the measuring, so tests, lint configuration, type-check configuration, benchmark definitions and the replay harness all live outside the model's write scope. That converts most of the gaming surface from trivial to hard. The gaming catalogue, recorded so the write-scope rule is understood rather than taken on faith: test pass rate is gamed by weakening an assertion, adding a skip marker, wrapping the call in try/except, or editing the test; coverage by writing tests that execute lines and assert nothing; lint and type-check counts by adding suppressions or loosening the rule; a wall-clock benchmark by memoising its exact input, moving work to import time so it falls outside the timed region, or shrinking the workload; bundle size by deferring a module so it leaves the measured bundle while still being downloaded; cyclomatic complexity by splitting one function into five that each call the next; and line count and duplication by compressing into dense cleverness, or extracting a shared helper with nine flags that is worse than the duplication it replaced.
epics.acceptance_criteria:
Sequencing: crawl hive-health and produce the behaviour manifest, with Daniel marking which captured behaviours are bugs rather than requirements; build the differential runner that pins the database, runs two code versions against it and diffs shape and computed output; build the duplication and token counter over the repo; stand up dsh as a third adapter matching whichever of the two existing template shapes it fits; wire the build loop with a container holding the manifest only, the small model building the throwaway, the oracle grading conformance and a large model repairing harness then scaffolding; and defer indefinitely the fine-tune and any recursion that depends on it.

Non-goals: features, bug fixes and UX changes, since the loop refactors and nothing else; converting the captured behaviour into hand-written tests as a precondition; and rewriting the existing test suites as a precondition, since test quality is a real problem and a separate project that does not gate this one.
epics.qa_tests:
Two risks worth holding. Without a behaviour oracle, the cheapest way to reduce duplicated tokens is to delete working code. And a replay oracle only covers behaviour someone exercised during capture, so code paths never hit are unprotected and are exactly where the model will be most free.

Five open questions: what exactly the fixed smoke build is and which tools it must exercise; how the throwaway target is reset between runs, a fresh container each night or a rolling codebase the builder continues from; what counts as identical in the oracle when a response carries timestamps, UUIDs or ordering that legitimately varies; what drives the crawler through authenticated, stateful flows that need a click order rather than a link list; and how many consecutive nights with no new findings end a campaign.

features.title: The oracle — recorded behaviour, reviewed as prose
features.description:
The behaviour oracle is a replay harness: capture real requests, responses, database queries and rendered output from the running system before a change, replay them after, and assert they come back identical. It asserts everything observable rather than the subset somebody thought to write a test for.

The capture is produced by a crawl and reviewed as prose before it is trusted. A crawler walks the running app — every link, every control, every state transition — and records what happens, producing two artefacts from one pass. The raw captures are the mechanical oracle, usable from night one with no hand-written tests in front of them: a golden master to replay, diff and fail on difference. The prose behaviour manifest is the same information written as 'when this happens, this happens', and it exists to be read by a human — because a golden master alone enshrines whatever the app does today, bugs included, as required behaviour. The manifest is where a captured behaviour gets marked as a bug rather than a requirement and excluded from the oracle. Hand-written tests derived from the manifest are a later, optional layer aimed at the inner mechanics a crawl cannot reach; they are not a precondition, because the capture is already executable and converting every captured behaviour into hand-authored test code first turns a night-one deliverable into a months-long project.
features.requirements:
The oracle compares shape, and compares the two versions against each other — two layers, and neither one remembers a value. Shape: the manifest and the capture record structure, never data — 'the home page shows a health score in a circular gauge, the point difference against yesterday, and a sentence about the day', not the score, not the difference, not the sentence; a test asserting that 58 equals 58 protects nothing and is exactly what makes most generated tests worthless. Value: correctness of computation is checked by differential run rather than by a stored constant — the old code and the new code are run against the same data at the same instant and their outputs diffed against each other, so data drift stops mattering because both sides see the same drift, and a refactor that quietly breaks the scoring maths is caught even though no snapshot of a correct score exists anywhere; shape diffing alone is blind to that class, which in a scoring app is the largest class. This dissolves the live-versus-fixture question: the capture runs against the live instance with the database pinned for the duration of a paired run.

The loop's blast radius is unrestricted, so the manifest's coverage must not be. The loop may touch whatever a fix legitimately requires, across any number of files, because consolidation is cross-file by nature and a UI behaviour is often a transition between pages rather than one page's contents. That forces the sequencing: if the loop may edit anything but the oracle only covers the home screen, every unwatched page can break in silence. So the crawl and manifest must cover the whole of hive-health before the first night runs. They are the first deliverable, and they are worth having on their own even if the loop is never built — a reviewed prose description of what the app actually does today does not currently exist.
features.acceptance_criteria: The first target is hive-health, because it is the only candidate with a real crawlable web UI. hive-edge-mind-skippy is HTTP, websocket and a terminal with no page to walk, so it is a later target captured at the API level rather than by crawl. The existing test suites run as a second, cheaper gate — they are already there and a failure is still a failure — but they are not the oracle and their quality is not a prerequisite, because making the oracle depend on them would turn a repo-wide test rewrite into a blocker in front of the MVP and would inherit exactly the blind spots that let regressions through in the first place.
features.qa_tests: The differential run is what catches broken computation with no stored constant anywhere. The shape layer must never record a value, which is testable: a manifest entry carrying a number is a defect rather than extra rigour.

stories.title: Crawl hive-health and produce the behaviour manifest
stories.description: The first deliverable, and worth having on its own. Daniel reviews it and marks which captured behaviours are bugs rather than requirements. The whole app, not the home screen, because the loop's blast radius is unrestricted.
stories.requirements: Every link, every control, every state transition. Shape only, never values.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A reviewed prose description of what the app actually does today, which does not currently exist.
stories.qa_tests: A manifest entry records structure and no value. A behaviour marked as a bug is excluded from the oracle. Shipped: the walkthrough and manifest landed as hive-health PRs #26 and #27, with sixteen views, fifty-two behaviours, nine bugs and six uncovered.

stories.title: Build the differential runner
stories.description: Pin the database, run two code versions against it at the same instant, and diff shape and computed output against each other rather than against a stored constant.
stories.requirements: Both layers. The database pinned for the duration of a paired run.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A refactor that quietly breaks the scoring maths is caught with no snapshot of a correct score existing anywhere.
stories.qa_tests: Two versions run against one pinned database produce diffable output. A deliberate change to the scoring maths is caught. Data drift between runs does not produce a false difference, because both sides see the same drift.

stories.title: Answer what counts as identical when a response legitimately varies
stories.description: An open question. Timestamps, UUIDs and ordering that legitimately varies.
stories.requirements: A rule, so a legitimate variance is not read as a regression.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The oracle does not fail on a fresh UUID.
stories.qa_tests: A response differing only in a timestamp or a UUID compares equal. One differing in an ordering that is genuinely unstable compares equal; one differing in an ordering the app promises does not.

stories.title: Answer what drives the crawler through authenticated stateful flows
stories.description: An open question. Flows that need a click order rather than a link list.
stories.requirements: A mechanism for ordered, stateful traversal.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The crawl reaches behind the login and through multi-step flows.
stories.qa_tests: A flow requiring a specific click order is reached. The switch-regression note is the reason this matters: a one-tap unconfirmed destructive action under a list of conversations is a UI defect no unit test would have caught and no captured page state would have caught either — only a crawl that presses the button and notices what it costs.

features.title: The mechanical reward
features.description: The reward is mechanical and the model only supplies taste. A model's opinion cannot be the reward signal — training on it is training on taste with extra steps. The reward is a number produced by tooling the model cannot edit, and the judge's role is narrowed to the dimension no tool can measure: whether an abstraction is real or a nine-flag monster, and whether the result is comprehensible.
features.requirements:
Duplication is the primary metric: AST-normalised token-level duplicate detection over the whole repo yields a real number — duplicated token count and its share of total tokens — which is mechanical, is exactly the defect AI-generated code actually has, and reducing it is the stated goal. Secondary mechanical figures: total token count, import-time work, and p50 latency on recorded traces.

Behaviour-preserving only: the overnight loop never adds a feature, fixes a bug, or changes anything a user could observe, and any behavioural difference is by definition a failed pass. That is what makes the verifier a diff rather than a judge.

A pass must clear a minimum gain to count as a success. Retrying until the oracle is happy has an obvious degenerate solution — make the change smaller and smaller until it changes nothing — so a behaviour-preserving change that reduces no duplication and no token count is recorded as neutral rather than as a win, and never becomes a positive training example.
features.acceptance_criteria: The counter is outside the model's write scope, because every metric is gameable precisely when the model can edit the thing measuring it.
features.qa_tests: The duplication count must be reproducible independent of file order, absolute paths and the counter's working directory — otherwise the number is not a measurement. The gain floor is testable at its boundary: just under records neutral, just over records accepted.

stories.title: Build the duplication and token counter over the repo
stories.description: AST-normalised token-level duplicate detection yielding duplicated token count and its share of total tokens. Plus total token count, import-time work, and p50 latency on recorded traces.
stories.requirements: Mechanical, and outside the model's write scope.
stories.acceptance_criteria: One number per run, reproducible.
stories.qa_tests: The same tree counted from two directories agrees, as does the same tree with its files enumerated in reverse, and the same tree moved to a different absolute path. Without that, the number is not a measurement.

stories.title: Enforce the gain floor so a no-op scores neutral
stories.description: A behaviour-preserving change that reduces no duplication and no token count is neutral rather than a win, and never becomes a positive training example. The floor is configurable.
stories.requirements: A third outcome, distinct from accepted and rejected.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The degenerate solution of shrinking the change until it changes nothing earns nothing.
stories.qa_tests: A gain one unit under the floor records neutral; one unit over records accepted. Changing the floor moves the boundary.

features.title: The ledger replaces file rotation
features.description: The no-repeat rotation is dropped. It was solving fixation, and the minimum-gain rule already solves it: duplication is counted repo-wide, so a model returning to a file it has already tightened finds nothing left to reduce, scores neutral and gets no credit. The economics rotate it without a rule forbidding anything — and a hard one-file limit would forbid the cross-file consolidation that is the whole point.
features.requirements: What replaces it is a ledger the next pass reads: every file visited, what was attempted, what the oracle said, and what gain it produced. A file whose recent visits all scored neutral drops down the priority order. One cheap cap remains, so a night cannot become one file: at most one accepted change per file per night.
features.acceptance_criteria: Fixation is solved by economics rather than by a prohibition that would also forbid the cross-file work.
features.qa_tests: With a seeded ledger where one file has several neutral visits, the next target is a different file. With an empty ledger, selection still produces a target. A second accepted change to a file already changed that night is refused.

stories.title: Write every pass to the ledger and read it for the next target
stories.description: File visited, what was attempted, what the oracle said, and the gain. A repeatedly-neutral file drops down the order.
stories.requirements: Read by the next pass, not just written.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The loop stops re-attempting files it has learned nothing from.
stories.qa_tests: A seeded ledger with a repeatedly-neutral file changes the next target. An empty ledger still yields one.

stories.title: Cap accepted changes at one per file per night
stories.description: The one cheap cap that remains, so a night cannot become one file.
stories.requirements: Accepted changes only — rejected and neutral attempts are not capped.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No file carries two accepted changes from one night.
stories.qa_tests: Two passes both producing an accepted change to one file result in one commit, with the second recorded with its reason.

features.title: Failure as signal, inside a time budget
features.description: A pass that breaks the oracle is not thrown away. The attempt, the reasoning and the failure are recorded, and the model tries a different approach with its own failures in front of it. Ten dead ends followed by one that works is a better training trace than one clean success, and on a local model the cost is electricity rather than tokens.
features.requirements: The loop runs inside a fixed nightly window — the dreaming hours, provisionally midnight to four. Nothing that still fails the oracle at the end of the window is committed or run live; it is kept as a negative record and the file is marked as having resisted.
features.acceptance_criteria: A night's accepted work lands on a branch with a report, never on master and never on the running app.
features.qa_tests: The window is driven by injected time rather than by waiting. A pass still failing at the close is kept as a negative record rather than discarded, which is what makes the trace worth collecting later.

stories.title: Record failed attempts and retry with the failures in context
stories.description: The attempt, the reasoning and the failure recorded, with the model trying a different approach with its own failures in front of it.
stories.requirements: The failures reach the retry's context.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Ten dead ends followed by one that works is a kept trace rather than a discarded night.
stories.qa_tests: A retry's prompt carries the prior failure. The negative records survive the night.

stories.title: Run inside a fixed nightly window and mark resisting files
stories.description: Provisionally midnight to four. Nothing still failing at the close is committed or run live; it is kept as a negative record and the file is marked as having resisted.
stories.requirements: A hard window, with resisted marked rather than silently dropped.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Nothing uncommitted reaches the running app.
stories.qa_tests: Driven by injected time: a pass still failing at the close is recorded as resisted and nothing is committed. Master's HEAD is unmoved.

features.title: Daniel is the judge, and the merge button is the label
features.description:
No model judge in the MVP, and no every-tenth-pass large-model review. The oracle rules on behaviour, the duplication count rules on gain, and the only thing left — whether an abstraction is real or a nine-flag monster that deduplicates on paper and ruins the code — is decided at the morning review.

Each accept and each reject, paired with the attempt that produced it, is a human preference label. That is the training signal, produced free as a byproduct of a review that was wanted anyway, and better than a judge model's guess at taste. A model judge returns only when Daniel stops reading diffs.
features.requirements: Review before anything runs: a night's accepted work lands on a branch with a report, never on master and never on the running app, and Daniel reads it in the morning and merges. Full autonomy is the intended destination once the loop has earned it rather than the starting configuration.
features.acceptance_criteria: Every merge and every reject is captured as a labelled pair against the attempt that produced it.
features.qa_tests: The label is the merge decision, which needs no model and no scoring. What is testable is that each decision is recorded against its attempt so a later training set can be assembled from them.

stories.title: Land each night's accepted work on a branch with a report
stories.description: Never master, never the running app. Daniel reads and merges in the morning.
stories.requirements: A branch per night and a report naming each accepted pass, its gain and where to look.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Nothing runs live without a human merge.
stories.qa_tests: After a night, master is unmoved and the branch holds one commit per accepted pass with a report beside it.

stories.title: Capture each merge and reject as a preference label
stories.description: Paired with the attempt that produced it. Free as a byproduct of a review that was wanted anyway, and better than a judge model's guess at taste.
stories.requirements: Recorded against the attempt identifier.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A training set can be assembled from the review history.
stories.qa_tests: A merge and a reject each produce a labelled record naming the attempt. A model judge returns only when Daniel stops reading diffs, so the absence of one is the design rather than a gap.

features.title: The harness candidate and the two builders
features.description:
The harness candidate is dsh: MIT, plugin-everything, with a headless command and a minimal benchmark mode. The requirements it has to meet are the ones this repo's adapter contract already implies — structured tool definitions rather than curl-via-skills, because local mid-tier models hallucinate the latter and narrate fabricated results; conversation resume by id; and either a per-turn process or a long-lived stream so it fits one of the two existing template shapes. Hermes is explicitly rejected as the vehicle: too large, and its plugin mechanism diverges from how the Claude and Codex adapters work, so nothing learned about it transfers.

Hard fork, no upstream relationship: dsh is taken as source, renamed, and committed to a new repository with no remote pointing at DeepSeek and no expectation of ever pulling from it. Nothing is reported upstream and nothing is waited on. Anything of theirs worth having later is read out of their repo by hand and applied deliberately. MIT permits this outright, and the licence and attribution travel with the fork. The one discipline the fork needs is recording the exact upstream commit it was taken from in the new repo's README — without it, going back later to see if there is anything worth having means reading a diff against nothing, which is how a fork stops being harvestable within a month. It costs one line. Forking a two-week-old developer preview means owning every bug it currently has, which is normally an argument against; here it is the point, because finding and fixing those bugs is the work.
features.requirements:
Two builders, and only agreement counts as a harness bug. The build runs against two models rather than one, and a failure is attributed to the harness only when both hit it — a failure on one model alone is that model's own. This is the only cheap way to make the attribution honest, because otherwise a large model repairs adapters in response to one weak model's idiosyncrasies and hardens the harness against a ghost. The pair, both already on the box and both fitting in the A6000's 48 GB at once at about 35 GB together, both declaring tool support and both carrying a 262,144 token context so the manifest and a growing codebase fit: a 27.3B dense Q4 model at 17 GB, the newest thing local, and a 30.5B coder-tuned one at 18 GB. Deliberately not the 120B at 65 GB, because it spills off the card and a build loop running partly on CPU turns a night into a week; and deliberately not the sub-10B models, because their failures would be their own rather than the harness's.

The stack is fixed per campaign rather than forever. A harness's tools are OS-level rather than language-level — read, write, edit, glob, grep, shell — so the same harness builds .NET and Angular at work and Python here, and a missing tool is almost never language-specific, which means a tool gap found in one stack transfers to every stack. Two things are still stack-shaped. The sandbox has to contain the toolchain the builder chose, and free choice means either preinstalling every toolchain or giving the builder a network path to fetch one — and the network is closed deliberately, because that is what stops it reading the original implementation, so a builder that decides on Rust inside a Python image fails for reasons that are neither the harness nor the model. And the scaffolding: phase two improves prompts, standing rules and skills, which are stack-specific by nature, since 'run the linter before claiming done' names a linter, so improvements only accumulate if consecutive runs are in the same stack. The agreement rule also needs comparable work, because two models failing in two different languages is two unrelated failures wearing one label. So a campaign fixes the stack and its image, runs until it stops producing new findings, and a later campaign changes both — generality comes from running several campaigns. Campaign one matches hive-health itself: Python 3.12, FastAPI on uvicorn, Jinja2 templates, and a single-page vanilla-JS front end with a service worker, with no build step and no framework.
features.acceptance_criteria: dsh stands up as a third adapter matching whichever of the two existing template shapes it fits. That has since happened — the adapter is merged and Cypher runs it live.
features.qa_tests: The agreement rule is the one that keeps the harness from being hardened against a ghost: a failure only one model hits is that model's own. That is testable as a rule about attribution rather than as code — a repair triggered by a single-model failure is the defect.

stories.title: Fork dsh with its upstream commit recorded
stories.description: DONE. Taken at 47f9438, MIT, maintained independently with no upstream remote. The pin is in the README — without it, going back later means reading a diff against nothing.
stories.requirements: The exact upstream commit in the new repo's README. One line.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The fork stays harvestable.
stories.qa_tests: The README names the commit. A diff against it resolves.

stories.title: Stand up dsh as a third adapter
stories.description: DONE. Matching the per-turn template shape. Merged as hive_mind PR #260, and Cypher runs it live.
stories.requirements: Structured tool definitions, resume by id, and one of the two existing template shapes.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A dsh mind takes a turn through the adapter.
stories.qa_tests: Covered by the adapter's own 36 tests. The resume-by-id half was gate zero for everything downstream.

stories.title: Run the build against two models and attribute only agreement to the harness
stories.description: A failure on one model alone is that model's own. Otherwise a large model hardens the harness against a ghost.
stories.requirements: The 27.3B dense and the 30.5B coder-tuned pair, both fitting the card together at about 35 GB.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No repair is triggered by a single-model failure.
stories.qa_tests: A failure reproduced on both models is attributed to the harness; one reproduced on neither or only one is not. The attribution rule is the test.

stories.title: Fix the stack and the image per campaign
stories.description: Campaign one is Python 3.12, FastAPI on uvicorn, Jinja2, and a single-page vanilla-JS front end with a service worker — no build step, no framework. The network is closed deliberately, so the image must contain the toolchain.
stories.requirements: One stack per campaign, with the image containing its toolchain.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A builder cannot fail for reasons that are neither the harness nor the model.
stories.qa_tests: A build in the campaign's stack completes. A build attempting a toolchain the image lacks fails with that named as the cause rather than as a model failure.

stories.title: Answer how many consecutive no-finding nights end a campaign
stories.description: An open question, and the thing that decides when to change the stack.
stories.requirements: A number.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A campaign ends on a rule rather than on boredom.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifact is the number.

features.title: The log, the review passes and the repair model
features.description: The log is the artifact, and it records successes too. The builder runs to the end of its window rather than halting on the first error, every turn is logged whole — the model's prose, its tool calls with full input, every tool result, and the user-side prompts — and the reviewing model reads that log afterwards rather than watching live. Successes are logged as deliberately as failures, because a model that used the wrong tool and got a clean result produces no error at all, and an error-only log makes that class of finding invisible. This is nearly free: the harness's own transcript is already this record, and the activity-blocks shape in the edge repo already demonstrates it — every block type, each capped tail-first with a trimmed marker. Findings are ranked by how early they appeared, and the repair model acts only on the earliest few, so a cascade of downstream failures caused by one real bug does not produce a dozen repairs to imaginary ones.
features.requirements:
Errors are extracted mechanically; only wrongness needs a model. Finding a tool call that errored requires no inference — a transcript's tool-result entries carry an error flag and a shell tool carries an exit code, so a script pulls every one of them out with the surrounding turns, for free, in seconds; spending a model on that is spending inference on a question the data structure already answers, which is the harness-native rule this repo already runs on. What genuinely needs a model is the other class, and it is the one worth having: the tool call that succeeded while being the wrong thing to do — wrong tool for the job, a skill that should have been read and was not, a fabricated result narrated instead of a call actually made — none of which is greppable. So the review is two passes: a script extracts every error and non-zero exit with context, cheaply and completely; then a model reads the successful turns looking for wrongness, scoped against the manifest's unmet requirements rather than reading a whole night end to end. The judgment pass starts on a local model, since the 27.3B carries a 262,144 token window, costs electricity, and this classification is the same job the hive's sub-minds already do well on every turn — escalation to a paid model is a decision made after seeing it fail rather than before.

The repair model is a frontier model. Repair runs on a large paid model, because it is the one step where quality is load-bearing: it writes harness code every later night depends on, and a local model producing a plausible-looking bad adapter poisons every run after it. Extraction, judgment and building all stay local; only repair is paid.
features.acceptance_criteria: The harness needs its own regression gate. The oracle grades the app rather than the harness, so a frontier model rewriting an adapter at three in the morning has nothing checking that the harness still works — and the failure mode is a harness that cannot start, discovered the following evening after a night of nothing. So every repair is followed by a fixed smoke task the harness must still pass: one small, unchanging build the harness is known to complete, run end to end with every tool exercised at least once. A repair that breaks the smoke task halts the run, and the broken repair is left in place, uncommitted, with the smoke failure beside it, and the night ends there — because a discarded fix from a paid model is worse than a lost night, since the discard is silent and the lost night is not. The halt raises a notification through the hive's existing notify path so it is read in the morning rather than discovered a day later.
features.qa_tests: The mechanical extraction needs no model and is therefore testable directly: every error flag and non-zero exit in a scripted transcript is pulled out with its surrounding turns, and none is missed. The wrongness pass is a mind's judgement, read rather than asserted — grading it with a regex would be testing the wrong thing.

stories.title: Log every turn whole, successes included
stories.description: The model's prose, its tool calls with full input, every tool result, and the user-side prompts. Successes as deliberately as failures, because a wrong tool with a clean result produces no error at all and an error-only log makes that class invisible.
stories.requirements: Every block type, capped tail-first with a trimmed marker — the activity-blocks shape already in the edge repo.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The reviewing model can read a night afterwards rather than watching live.
stories.qa_tests: A night's log contains successful turns with their full tool input and results. An oversized block is capped tail-first and marked trimmed rather than dropped.

stories.title: Extract every error and non-zero exit mechanically
stories.description: A script, not a model. Tool-result entries carry an error flag and a shell tool carries an exit code, so this is free and complete in seconds — spending inference on it is spending inference on a question the data structure already answers.
stories.requirements: Complete, with surrounding turns for context.
stories.acceptance_criteria: No error is missed and no model is involved.
stories.qa_tests: A scripted transcript's every error flag and non-zero exit is pulled out with context. A missed one is the defect; a false positive is cheap.

stories.title: Have a model read the successful turns for wrongness
stories.description: The class that is not greppable: wrong tool for the job, a skill that should have been read and was not, a fabricated result narrated instead of a call actually made. Scoped against the manifest's unmet requirements rather than reading a whole night end to end. Starts on a local model, with escalation to a paid one a decision made after seeing it fail.
stories.requirements: Scoped, and local first.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The wrong-but-clean class of finding stops being invisible.
stories.qa_tests: Judged by reading the model's findings against the log, not asserted. A regex over this would be testing the wrong thing.

stories.title: Rank findings by how early they appeared and repair only the earliest few
stories.description: So a cascade of downstream failures caused by one real bug does not produce a dozen repairs to imaginary ones.
stories.requirements: Ranked by position in the night.
stories.acceptance_criteria: One real bug produces one repair rather than twelve.
stories.qa_tests: A scripted night where one early failure causes several later ones yields a repair list naming the early one.

stories.title: Run repair on a frontier model
stories.description: The one step where quality is load-bearing, because it writes harness code every later night depends on and a local model producing a plausible-looking bad adapter poisons every run after it. Extraction, judgment and building stay local; only repair is paid.
stories.requirements: A large paid model for repair alone.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The paid spend is confined to the step that justifies it.
stories.qa_tests: The cost per night is attributable to repair alone. The other three passes make no paid call.

stories.title: Add the harness's own smoke gate after every repair
stories.description: One small, unchanging build the harness is known to complete, run end to end with every tool exercised at least once. A repair that breaks it halts the run, leaving the broken repair in place uncommitted with the failure beside it, and raising a notification through the existing notify path — because a discarded fix from a paid model is worse than a lost night, since the discard is silent and the lost night is not.
stories.requirements: Every tool exercised at least once. The halt notified rather than logged.
stories.acceptance_criteria: A harness that cannot start is discovered that morning rather than the following evening.
stories.qa_tests: A deliberately broken repair halts the run with the failure recorded beside it and a notification sent. The broken repair is still on disk, uncommitted — discarding it silently is the failure this avoids.

stories.title: Answer what the fixed smoke build is and which tools it must exercise
stories.description: An open question, and the gate depends on it.
stories.requirements: A specific build, and a tool list.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Unchanging, so a failure means the harness changed rather than the task.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifact is the specification. An unchanging task is what makes the gate meaningful.

features.title: The build loop and the deferred fine-tune
features.description: Step five of the sequencing: wire the build loop, with a container holding the manifest only, the small model building the throwaway, the oracle grading conformance, and a large model repairing harness then scaffolding. Step six is deferred indefinitely: the fine-tune and any recursion that depends on it.
features.requirements: The container's filesystem holds the empty project directory and the behaviour manifest and nothing else — no checkout, no git remote, no network path to the original — and the oracle runs outside it. Nothing is hidden by prompt instruction, because nothing is reachable. The phases are strictly ordered: harden the harness, then the scaffolding, with no training; freeze both; and only then collect traces, because from that point a success is attributable to the model and a failure is the model's own.
features.acceptance_criteria: The fine-tune is rejection-sampling fine-tuning — run many attempts, keep the ones that pass the oracle, train on those — and it is deferred indefinitely, better suited to the work setting with more developers on it than to this workstation. Nothing in the design depends on it happening.
features.qa_tests: The isolation is testable by trying to reach the original from inside the container: no checkout, no remote, no network path. That is what makes the reward un-hackable rather than a prompt instruction nobody can verify.

stories.title: Wire the build loop with manifest-only isolation
stories.description: A container holding the empty project directory and the manifest and nothing else, with the oracle outside it.
stories.requirements: No checkout, no remote, no network path to the original.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Nothing needs hiding by prompt instruction, because nothing is reachable.
stories.qa_tests: From inside the container, the original implementation is unreachable by any route. A prompt instruction not to look would be unverifiable, which is why this is filesystem and network rather than wording.

stories.title: Answer how the throwaway target is reset between runs
stories.description: An open question: a fresh container each night, or a rolling codebase the builder continues from.
stories.requirements: A decision, because it changes what a night's score means.
stories.acceptance_criteria: Decided before the loop runs nightly.
stories.qa_tests: Not code. The artifact is the decision. A rolling codebase makes a night's score cumulative rather than independent, which changes how the ledger reads.

stories.title: Freeze the harness and scaffolding before collecting any traces
stories.description: The strict phase ordering. Every harness fix makes the small model succeed for reasons that are not in the model, so a trace collected while the harness is still being repaired teaches the model nothing it can carry.
stories.requirements: Both frozen, and the freeze recorded.
stories.acceptance_criteria: From the freeze onward, a success is attributable to the model and a failure is the model's own.
stories.qa_tests: No trace is collected before the freeze. The freeze point is recorded against the harness revision, so a trace's provenance is checkable.

stories.title: Defer the fine-tune indefinitely
stories.description: Rejection-sampling fine-tuning is a real technique rather than a fantasy, but it is better suited to the work setting with more developers on it than to this workstation. Nothing in the design depends on it happening.
stories.requirements: Deferred, with the design not depending on it.
stories.acceptance_criteria: The harness is the deliverable.
stories.qa_tests: Not applicable. The absence is deliberate rather than an omission.
